users: Online customers, customer support, warehouse and inventory staff, finance and payment operations, product management, software engineers, and operations staff.
non_functional_requirements: Support up to 50,000 concurrent users during peak campaigns

blueprint.rationale: Combines domain‑driven service boundaries with asynchronous event‑driven communication to meet high concurrency, scalability, and availability requirements while keeping user‑facing interactions low‑latency via synchronous APIs. Managed AWS services and serverless compute are used to control costs in the absence of a fixed budget.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Customers browse, search, add items to carts, and place orders; they expect fast, reliable experiences even during peak campaigns. Staff manage product catalogs, inventory, and order fulfillment; finance processes payments. The platform must support up to 50,000 concurrent users, stay highly available during traffic spikes, and scale automatically while keeping operational costs reasonable.
blueprint.technical_view: Stateless services are containerized on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. API Gateway exposes REST/GraphQL endpoints for the web UI. Internal workflows use an SNS/SQS Event Bus for asynchronous communication. Each service owns a DynamoDB table; the Search Service uses Amazon OpenSearch; Redis (ElastiCache) caches hot product data. Email and SMS notifications are sent via managed Amazon SES and SNS services. All components are managed services that auto‑scale and provide multi‑AZ resilience.

constraints_addressed: Cost efficiency (use of managed services, serverless compute, and autoscaling to keep spend proportional to load)
assumptions: All AWS managed services are available in the selected region.
Stateless services can be containerized on Fargate.
Eventual consistency is acceptable for inventory updates after order placement.
open_risks: Increased operational complexity due to many microservices and event pipelines.
Potential cost overruns if autoscaling thresholds are not tuned.
Eventual consistency may cause short‑lived stock‑out anomalies.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Adopt Domain-Driven Design bounded contexts for service boundaries
adrs.context: Need to define clear service boundaries for scalability, maintainability, and independent deployment.
adrs.decision: Decompose the system into services aligned with DDD bounded contexts: User Account, Product Catalog, Search, Cart, Order, Payment, Inventory, Notification.
adrs.rationale: DDD aligns services with business capabilities, reduces coupling, and supports independent scaling as required for peak traffic.

adrs.title: ADR-002: Use service‑owned polyglot persistence with DynamoDB and OpenSearch
adrs.context: Each service requires its own data store that matches its access patterns and scalability needs.
adrs.decision: Each microservice owns a private DynamoDB table; the Search Service uses Amazon OpenSearch for full‑text search.
adrs.rationale: Service‑owned stores prevent accidental coupling and enable independent schema evolution; DynamoDB provides horizontal scalability, while OpenSearch satisfies search requirements.
alternatives_considered: All services using the same NoSQL store

adrs.title: ADR-003: Hybrid integration style – synchronous API for front‑end, asynchronous events for internal processes
adrs.context: User‑facing interactions need low latency, while internal workflows benefit from decoupling and scalability.
adrs.decision: Expose REST/GraphQL endpoints via API Gateway for all external calls; use SNS/SQS Event Bus for order, inventory, and payment events between services.
adrs.rationale: Synchronous APIs give immediate feedback to customers; asynchronous events improve throughput and fault tolerance for background processing.
alternatives_considered: Fully synchronous request‑response across all services
negative_consequences: Added complexity of managing both sync and async paths

adrs.title: ADR-004: Stateless services with AWS autoscaling and managed data stores for high availability
adrs.context: The platform must handle large traffic spikes without manual capacity planning.
adrs.decision: Deploy services as stateless containers on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer; rely on DynamoDB, ElastiCache, and OpenSearch which provide built‑in autoscaling and multi‑AZ replication.
adrs.rationale: Stateless compute enables rapid horizontal scaling; managed data stores remove operational burden and guarantee high availability.
alternatives_considered: Self‑managed EC2 instances with manual scaling
Monolithic deployment on a single VM
negative_consequences: Higher per‑request cost of managed services

adrs.title: ADR-005: Use serverless and managed services to optimize cost
adrs.context: No fixed monetary budget is defined; cost efficiency must be a primary design driver.
adrs.decision: Leverage AWS managed services (Fargate, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, OpenSearch, SNS/SQS, SES) and serverless compute (Lambda) to ensure that capacity and spend scale proportionally with load, avoiding over‑provisioning.
adrs.rationale: Managed services provide pay‑as‑you‑go pricing, automatic scaling, and reduced operational labor, aligning spend with actual usage and satisfying the budget constraint.
alternatives_considered: Self‑managed EC2 fleet with manual scaling
Provisioned capacity on traditional relational databases
negative_consequences: Potentially higher per‑unit cost at very low utilization
Vendor lock‑in to AWS managed services

components.name: Frontend UI
components.purpose: Customer‑facing web application for browsing, searching, cart management, and checkout.
components.description: A React single‑page application delivered via CDN, interacting with the backend through the API Gateway.
inputs: User HTTP requests (browsing, search, cart actions, checkout, order history)
scalability_considerations: Static assets cached at edge locations

components.name: Load Balancer
components.purpose: Distribute incoming HTTP traffic across API Gateway instances and provide health‑checking.
components.description: AWS Application Load Balancer operating in multiple AZs, terminating TLS and forwarding requests to the API Gateway.
outputs: Forwarded HTTP requests to API Gateway
scalability_considerations: Automatic scaling of load balancer capacity

components.name: API Gateway
components.purpose: Expose synchronous REST/GraphQL endpoints for all front‑end interactions.
components.description: AWS API Gateway routes HTTP requests to the appropriate backend services and handles request validation, throttling, and authentication.
scalability_considerations: Managed scaling to handle request bursts

components.name: User Account Service
components.purpose: Manage customer registration, authentication, profile updates, and password recovery.
components.description: Stateless service handling account CRUD operations, issuing JWTs, and persisting user data in its own DynamoDB table.
inputs: Account API calls from API Gateway

components.name: Product Catalog Service
components.purpose: Provide product information, categories, and availability data to the front‑end.
components.description: Stateless service exposing product browse APIs; reads product data from its DynamoDB table and writes inventory updates.
inputs: Product browse requests from API Gateway
scalability_considerations: Read‑heavy workload benefits from Redis cache

components.name: Search Service
components.purpose: Execute full‑text product searches and filter queries.
components.description: Stateless service that forwards search queries to the OpenSearch cluster and returns ranked results.
security_considerations: Sanitize query strings to prevent injection

components.name: Cart Service
components.purpose: Maintain a persistent shopping cart per customer across sessions.
components.description: Stateless service that stores cart state in DynamoDB; supports add, update, remove, and retrieval operations.
inputs: Cart manipulation requests from API Gateway
security_considerations: Validate product IDs against Product Catalog Service

components.name: Order Service
components.purpose: Create, persist, and manage customer orders and provide order history.
components.description: Stateless service that records orders, reserves inventory, emits OrderCreated events, and serves order‑history queries for customers.
inputs: Order history requests from API Gateway
security_considerations: Validate payment status before confirming order
scalability_considerations: Event‑driven order processing decouples load spikes

components.name: Payment Service
components.purpose: Process customer payments securely and report outcomes.
components.description: Stateless service that integrates with external payment providers, records transaction results, and publishes PaymentProcessed events.
security_considerations: TLS encryption for all external calls
scalability_considerations: Asynchronous event publishing avoids blocking checkout flow

components.name: Inventory Service
components.purpose: Track stock levels and enforce product availability constraints.
components.description: Stateless service that updates inventory counts, prevents overselling, and emits InventoryReserved events.
inputs: Inventory check requests from API Gateway
security_considerations: Validate order quantities against available stock
scalability_considerations: DynamoDB scales for high write throughput

components.name: Notification Service
components.purpose: Send email/SMS notifications for order confirmations, payment receipts, and shipment updates.
components.description: Consumes events from the Event Bus and triggers outbound messages via Amazon SES and SNS.
security_considerations: Ensure email content does not expose sensitive data
scalability_considerations: Lambda scales automatically with event volume

components.name: Event Bus
components.purpose: Provide asynchronous, decoupled communication between services.
components.description: Implemented with Amazon SNS topics and SQS queues; supports at‑least‑once delivery and fan‑out to multiple consumers.
outputs: Events delivered to Notification Service and other interested services
scalability_considerations: Managed service scales automatically with message volume

components.name: Data Store
components.purpose: Persist domain data for all services using DynamoDB.
components.description: A set of DynamoDB tables, each owned by a single service, providing low‑latency, highly available key‑value storage.
scalability_considerations: On‑demand capacity mode for unpredictable traffic
Global secondary indexes for query patterns

components.name: Cache
components.purpose: Accelerate read‑heavy product data and reduce DynamoDB load.
components.description: Redis cluster (ElastiCache) used for caching product listings and session data.
inputs: Cache get/set requests from API Gateway and services

components.name: Search Index
components.purpose: Store searchable product documents for full‑text queries.
components.description: OpenSearch domain containing indexed product data, refreshed from the Product Catalog Service.
inputs: Indexing updates from Product Catalog Service
outputs: Search result documents to Search Service

components.name: Email Service
components.purpose: Send transactional email notifications (order confirmations, receipts).
components.description: Managed Amazon SES service used by the Notification Service to deliver email messages.
inputs: Email message payloads from Notification Service
security_considerations: DKIM and SPF for email authenticity

components.name: SMS Service
components.purpose: Send transactional SMS notifications (order updates, alerts).
components.description: Managed Amazon SNS SMS capability used by the Notification Service to deliver short message alerts.
inputs: SMS message payloads from Notification Service
scalability_considerations: Managed service scales automatically with message volume

retrieved_knowledge.content:
Microservices architecture has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the promise of enhanced scalability, improved fault tolerance, and greater development agility [1]. By decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, independently deployable services, organizations can achieve better resource utilization, faster deployment cycles, and improved system resilience.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) patterns have gained particular attention in the context of microservices migration, especially for e-commerce systems where business processes are inherently event-oriented. Customer actions such as placing orders, updating profiles, or processing payments naturally translate to domain events that can drive system behavior [5]. The asynchronous nature of event-driven communication provides better decoupling between services, enhanced fault tolerance, and improved scalability compared to synchronous request-response patterns [4].

**b. High Load Scenarios:** Asynchronous patterns (message queues) demonstrate superior throughput and availability [4].

**c. Availability:** Event-driven architectures provide better fault tolerance and system availability under stress [4].

These findings suggest that e-commerce systems should employ hybrid approaches, using synchronous communication for real-time user interactions and asynchronous patterns for backend processing and inter-service communication.

**Solution mechanics:** The application is designed to be **stateless** — per AWS, it "does not need knowledge of previous interactions and does not store session information" locally on disk or in memory between requests. All session/user state is offloaded to an external, resilient, multi-zone store (e.g., Amazon ElastiCache/Redis, DynamoDB, or a database); anything that can be is passed in request parameters, headers, or tokens instead of stored server-side. Because no request depends on server-local state, **any** available instance can serve **any** request, so you scale out (add interchangeable instances — "scale-out") behind a load balancer, and instances can be replaced or terminated at will without availability impact. This enables autoscaling (add/remove instances on demand, distributed across Availability Zones for reliability) and serverless compute (AWS Lambda, Fargate) where any compute resource services any request.

The reviewed studies reveal several distinct approaches to monolith decomposition, each with specific advantages for e-commerce contexts.

**a. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Approaches:** Multiple studies emphasize Domain-Driven Design as a foundational approach for identifying service boundaries in e-commerce systems. Abgaz et al. [1] identify DDD as a critical component of their Monolith to Microservices Decomposition Framework (M2MDF), noting its effectiveness in creating business-aligned service boundaries. Kaloudis [6] reinforces this approach, demonstrating how DDD enables better service cohesion and reduced coupling. In e-commerce contexts, natural domain boundaries often align with business capabilities, such as customer management, product catalog, order processing, payment handling, and inventory management.

With a domain-driven microservices approach, each service uses the database that fits its data characteristics. Each microservice owns its private data store. This design prevents unintentional coupling between services and supports independent updates and deployments without coordinating changes across the system.

## 2.2 Monolithic and Microservices Architectures Comparison *(printed p. 478)*

In the e-commerce landscape, choosing between microservices and traditional monolithic architectures requires careful consideration of various factors. Monolithic architectures, characterized by their single, tightly coupled codebase. However, when e-commerce systems increase in size, they frequently face scalability and maintenance issues. Microservices provide an alternative approach by decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, self-contained services [6]. This decomposition results in fine-grained services, each focusing on a specific business capability. Scalability is one of the most major advantages of microservices. E-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic patterns, especially during promotions or seasonal events. Microservices enable organisations to scale individual services, ensuring that resources are deployed efficiently to manage workload properly.

NoSQL databases have been designed to favor scalability, performance, and availability over the 
consistency of relational databases. One important element of NoSQL databases is that they 
typically don’t enforce a strict schema. Data is distributed over partitions that can be scaled 
horizontally and is retrieved using partition keys.
Because individual microservices are designed to do one thing well, they typically have a simpliﬁed 
data model that might be well suited to NoSQL persistence. It is important to understand 
that NoSQL databases have diﬀerent access patterns than relational databases. For example, 
it's not possible to join tables. If this is necessary, the logic has to be implemented in the 
application. You can use Amazon DynamoDB to create a database table that can store and 
retrieve any amount of data and serve any level of request traﬃc. DynamoDB delivers single-

Event-Driven Communication:** Asynchronous event-driven patterns prove superior for e-commerce workloads, providing better scalability under high load conditions and improved fault tolerance [4][5]. The natural event-oriented nature of e-commerce business processes aligns well with event-driven architectures.

**d. Comprehensive Tooling:** Organizations benefit significantly from automated decomposition tools like Mono2Micro [10], which provide objective analysis of service boundaries and reduce subjective architectural decisions.

## DISCUSSION — 2. Performance Considerations *(printed p. 16)*

The performance analysis reveals nuanced trade-offs between synchronous and asynchronous communication patterns:

**a. Low Load Scenarios:** Synchronous patterns (gRPC, REST) provide better performance with lower latency [4].

**b. High Load Scenarios:** Asynchronous patterns (message queues) demonstrate superior throughput and availability [4].

## Scaling for traffic surges and catalog growth *(PDF p. 11)*

E-commerce platforms face unpredictable traffic surges and growing product catalogs.

The article describes two broad scaling approaches:

- **Vertical scaling:** increase the resources available to existing data nodes.
- **Horizontal scaling:** add more data nodes so indexing and search work can be distributed across more cluster capacity.

For traffic growth or increasing data volume, horizontal scaling can distribute load across nodes. Temporary additional replicas can also increase read throughput during high-traffic periods without requiring permanent capacity at the same level.

## Monitoring search quality and capacity *(PDF pp. 11-12)*

Search infrastructure should be monitored using workload and performance indicators rather than sized once and left unchanged.

features.name: Product browsing and search
features.description: Customers can discover products by browsing categories and searching with keywords, applying filters, and viewing paginated results.
features.scenario: A customer enters a keyword and selects filter options; the system returns a list of matching products within a reasonable time and allows navigation through result pages.
acceptance_criteria: Search returns results that match the entered keywords and selected filters.
Product list is displayed without errors and supports pagination.
Response time is perceived as acceptable by users under normal load.

features.name: Customer account management
features.description: Customers can create, authenticate, and maintain their personal accounts, including profile updates and password recovery.
features.scenario: A new user registers, verifies email, logs in, updates their address, and successfully resets their password using the recovery flow.
acceptance_criteria: Account creation completes and a verification email is sent.
Login succeeds with correct credentials and fails with incorrect ones.
Profile changes are persisted and visible on subsequent logins.
Password reset email is delivered and allows the user to set a new password.

features.name: Shopping cart management
features.description: Customers can add, modify, and remove items in a persistent shopping cart across sessions.
features.scenario: A logged‑in customer adds three different products, changes the quantity of one, removes another, then logs out and later returns to find the cart unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: Items added appear in the cart with correct quantities.
Quantity updates are reflected immediately.
Removed items no longer appear in the cart.
Cart contents persist after logout and subsequent login.

features.name: Order placement and processing
features.description: Customers can complete checkout, creating an order that is recorded and acknowledged.
features.scenario: A customer proceeds from cart to checkout, confirms shipping details, and submits the order; the system generates an order record and sends a confirmation email.
acceptance_criteria: Order is created with correct line items and totals.
Inventory is reserved for the ordered items.
A confirmation email containing order details is sent to the customer.
Order appears in the customer's order history.

features.name: Payment handling
features.description: The platform securely processes customer payments and reflects payment outcomes on orders.
features.scenario: During checkout, a customer enters valid payment information; the transaction is processed successfully and the order status changes to Paid. A declined payment results in an appropriate error message.
acceptance_criteria: Successful payment updates the order status to Paid and triggers a receipt email.
Declined or failed payment returns a clear error message without creating a charged order.
Sensitive payment data is never stored in plain text.

features.name: Inventory and availability management
features.description: Staff can manage stock levels, and the system reflects product availability to customers, preventing overselling.
features.scenario: An inventory manager updates the stock count for a product; the product page immediately shows the new availability, and attempts to purchase beyond available stock are blocked.
acceptance_criteria: Stock level changes are reflected on product detail pages in real time.
When inventory reaches zero, the product is shown as out‑of‑stock and cannot be added to the cart.
Order processing decrements inventory accurately.

features.name: Order status and history view
features.description: Customers can view a list of their past orders and the current status of each order.
features.scenario: A logged‑in customer navigates to the 'My Orders' page, sees a list of previous purchases with dates, totals, and status indicators such as 'Shipped' or 'Delivered'.
acceptance_criteria: All orders belonging to the customer are displayed in reverse chronological order.
Each order shows accurate status information matching the backend state.
Clicking an order reveals detailed line items and shipping information.

features.name: Peak concurrency support
features.description: The platform can sustain the required number of simultaneous users during high‑traffic campaigns.
features.scenario: During a simulated peak campaign, 50,000 concurrent virtual users browse products, add items to carts, and place orders without service degradation.
acceptance_criteria: All core user flows (browse, cart, checkout) remain functional with 50,000 concurrent users.
Error rates stay within acceptable limits and no critical failures occur.
System resources scale to meet the load without manual intervention.

features.name: High availability during peaks
features.description: The system remains reachable and operational throughout peak traffic periods.
features.scenario: While the platform experiences peak load, health‑check endpoints continuously report healthy status and no user reports an inability to access the site.
acceptance_criteria: All services report healthy status for the duration of the peak load test.
No downtime or loss of connectivity is observed by simulated users.
Failover mechanisms activate automatically if a component becomes unhealthy.

features.name: Responsive customer‑facing interactions
features.description: User‑visible operations respond quickly enough to be perceived as responsive under normal and peak conditions.
features.scenario: Customers perform typical actions (search, view product, add to cart) during both regular traffic and peak load; they do not experience noticeable lag or timeouts.
acceptance_criteria: User actions complete without timeouts or error pages.
Feedback from usability testing indicates interactions feel responsive.
No UI element remains in a loading state for an extended period.

features.name: Elastic scalability
features.description: The platform can automatically expand capacity as demand grows, without service interruption.
features.scenario: Traffic gradually increases from baseline to well beyond typical levels; the system automatically provisions additional compute and storage resources, and continues serving requests seamlessly.
acceptance_criteria: Scaling events are triggered automatically based on load metrics.
New resources are added without causing request failures or noticeable latency spikes.
After scaling, the system continues to meet functional and performance expectations.

Sensitive payment data is never stored in plain text.

features.name: Inventory and availability management
features.description: Staff can manage stock levels, and the system reflects product availability to customers, preventing overselling.
features.scenario: An inventory manager updates the stock count for a product; the product page immediately shows the new availability, and attempts to purchase beyond available stock are blocked.
acceptance_criteria: Stock level changes are reflected on product detail pages in real time.
When inventory reaches zero, the product is shown as out‑of‑stock and cannot be added to the cart.
Order processing decrements inventory accurately.

features.name: Order status and history view
features.description: Customers can view a list of their past orders and the current status of each order.
features.scenario: A logged‑in customer navigates to the 'My Orders' page, sees a list of previous purchases with dates, totals, and status indicators such as 'Shipped' or 'Delivered'.
acceptance_criteria: All orders belonging to the customer are displayed in reverse chronological order.
Each order shows accurate status information matching the backend state.
Clicking an order reveals detailed line items and shipping information.

features.name: Peak concurrency support
features.description: The platform can sustain the required number of simultaneous users during high‑traffic campaigns.
features.scenario: During a simulated peak campaign, 50,000 concurrent virtual users browse products, add items to carts, and place orders without service degradation.
acceptance_criteria: All core user flows (browse, cart, checkout) remain functional with 50,000 concurrent users.
Error rates stay within acceptable limits and no critical failures occur.
System resources scale to meet the load without manual intervention.

features.name: High availability during peaks
features.description: The system remains reachable and operational throughout peak traffic periods.
features.scenario: While the platform experiences peak load, health‑check endpoints continuously report healthy status and no user reports an inability to access the site.
acceptance_criteria: All services report healthy status for the duration of the peak load test.
No downtime or loss of connectivity is observed by simulated users.
Failover mechanisms activate automatically if a component becomes unhealthy.

features.name: Responsive customer‑facing interactions
features.description: User‑visible operations respond quickly enough to be perceived as responsive under normal and peak conditions.
features.scenario: Customers perform typical actions (search, view product, add to cart) during both regular traffic and peak load; they do not experience noticeable lag or timeouts.
acceptance_criteria: User actions complete without timeouts or error pages.
Feedback from usability testing indicates interactions feel responsive.
No UI element remains in a loading state for an extended period.

features.name: Elastic scalability
features.description: The platform can automatically expand capacity as demand grows, without service interruption.
features.scenario: Traffic gradually increases from baseline to well beyond typical levels; the system automatically provisions additional compute and storage resources, and continues serving requests seamlessly.
acceptance_criteria: Scaling events are triggered automatically based on load metrics.
New resources are added without causing request failures or noticeable latency spikes.
After scaling, the system continues to meet functional and performance expectations.

blueprint.rationale: Combines domain‑driven service boundaries with asynchronous event‑driven communication to meet high concurrency, scalability, and availability requirements while keeping user‑facing interactions low‑latency via synchronous APIs.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Customers browse, search, add items to carts, and place orders; they expect fast, reliable experiences even during peak campaigns. Staff manage product catalogs, inventory, and order fulfillment; finance processes payments. The platform must support up to 50,000 concurrent users, stay highly available during traffic spikes, and scale automatically while keeping operational costs reasonable.
blueprint.technical_view: The solution consists of domain‑aligned stateless services deployed on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. API Gateway exposes synchronous REST endpoints for the web UI. Internally services exchange domain events via an SNS/SQS Event Bus for order, inventory, and payment workflows. Each service owns its own DynamoDB table; the Search Service uses Amazon OpenSearch. A Redis (ElastiCache) cache accelerates product‑read traffic. All components are managed services, enabling horizontal autoscaling and built‑in high availability.
data_flows: Frontend UI → Load Balancer: HTTP traffic from browsers
Load Balancer → API Gateway: Forward HTTP requests
API Gateway → User Account Service: Account CRUD API calls
API Gateway → Product Catalog Service: Product browse API calls
API Gateway → Search Service: Search query API calls
API Gateway → Cart Service: Cart manipulation API calls
API Gateway → Order Service: Checkout request API call
API Gateway → Payment Service: Payment processing API call
API Gateway → Inventory Service: Inventory availability check API call
User Account Service → Data Store: Read/write user data
Product Catalog Service → Data Store: Read product data
Search Service → Search Index: Query OpenSearch index
Cart Service → Data Store: Persist cart state
Order Service → Data Store: Persist order data
Payment Service → Data Store: Persist payment transaction
Inventory Service → Data Store: Update stock levels
Order Service → Event Bus: Publish OrderCreated event
Inventory Service → Event Bus: Publish InventoryReserved event
Payment Service → Event Bus: Publish PaymentProcessed event
Event Bus → Notification Service: Deliver order and payment events
Notification Service → Email Service (External): Send confirmation emails
Data Store → Cache: Populate cache entries
API Gateway → Cache: Retrieve cached product data
constraints_addressed: Cost efficiency (use of managed services and autoscaling)
assumptions: All AWS managed services are available in the selected region.
Stateless services can be containerized on Fargate.
Eventual consistency is acceptable for inventory updates after order placement.
open_risks: Increased operational complexity due to many microservices and event pipelines.
Potential cost overruns if autoscaling thresholds are not tuned.
Eventual consistency may cause short‑lived stock‑out anomalies.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Adopt Domain-Driven Design bounded contexts for service boundaries
adrs.context: Need to define clear service boundaries for scalability, maintainability, and independent deployment.
adrs.decision: Decompose the system into services aligned with DDD bounded contexts: User Account, Product Catalog, Search, Cart, Order, Payment, Inventory, Notification.
adrs.rationale: DDD aligns services with business capabilities, reduces coupling, and supports independent scaling as required for peak traffic.

adrs.title: ADR-002: Use service‑owned polyglot persistence with DynamoDB and OpenSearch
adrs.context: Each service requires its own data store that matches its access patterns and scalability needs.
adrs.decision: Each microservice owns a private DynamoDB table; the Search Service uses Amazon OpenSearch for full‑text search.
adrs.rationale: Service‑owned stores prevent accidental coupling and enable independent schema evolution; DynamoDB provides horizontal scalability, while OpenSearch satisfies search requirements.
alternatives_considered: All services using the same NoSQL store

adrs.title: ADR-003: Hybrid integration style – synchronous API for front‑end, asynchronous events for internal processes
adrs.context: User‑facing interactions need low latency, while internal workflows benefit from decoupling and scalability.
adrs.decision: Expose REST/GraphQL endpoints via API Gateway for all external calls; use SNS/SQS Event Bus for order, inventory, and payment events between services.
adrs.rationale: Synchronous APIs give immediate feedback to customers; asynchronous events improve throughput and fault tolerance for background processing.
alternatives_considered: Fully synchronous request‑response across all services
negative_consequences: Added complexity of managing both sync and async paths

adrs.title: ADR-004: Stateless services with AWS autoscaling and managed data stores for high availability
adrs.context: The platform must handle large traffic spikes without manual capacity planning.
adrs.decision: Deploy services as stateless containers on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer; rely on DynamoDB, ElastiCache, and OpenSearch which provide built‑in autoscaling and multi‑AZ replication.
adrs.rationale: Stateless compute enables rapid horizontal scaling; managed data stores remove operational burden and guarantee high availability.
alternatives_considered: Self‑managed EC2 instances with manual scaling
Monolithic deployment on a single VM
negative_consequences: Higher per‑request cost of managed services

components.name: Frontend UI
components.purpose: Customer‑facing web application for browsing, searching, cart management, and checkout.
components.description: A React single‑page application delivered via CDN, interacting with the backend through the API Gateway.
inputs: User HTTP requests (browsing, search, cart actions, checkout)
scalability_considerations: Static assets cached at edge locations

components.name: Load Balancer
components.purpose: Distribute incoming HTTP traffic across API Gateway instances and provide health‑checking.
components.description: AWS Application Load Balancer operating in multiple AZs, terminating TLS and forwarding requests to the API Gateway.
outputs: Forwarded HTTP requests to API Gateway
scalability_considerations: Automatic scaling of load balancer capacity

components.name: API Gateway
components.purpose: Expose synchronous REST/GraphQL endpoints for all front‑end interactions.
components.description: AWS API Gateway routes HTTP requests to the appropriate backend services and handles request validation, throttling, and authentication.
scalability_considerations: Managed scaling to handle request bursts

components.name: User Account Service
components.purpose: Manage customer registration, authentication, profile updates, and password recovery.
components.description: Stateless service handling account CRUD operations, issuing JWTs, and persisting user data in its own DynamoDB table.
inputs: Account API calls from API Gateway

components.name: Product Catalog Service
components.purpose: Provide product information, categories, and availability data to the front‑end.
components.description: Stateless service exposing product browse APIs; reads product data from its DynamoDB table and writes inventory updates.
inputs: Product browse requests from API Gateway
scalability_considerations: Read‑heavy workload benefits from Redis cache

components.name: Search Service
components.purpose: Execute full‑text product searches and filter queries.
components.description: Stateless service that forwards search queries to the OpenSearch cluster and returns ranked results.
security_considerations: Sanitize query strings to prevent injection

components.name: Cart Service
components.purpose: Maintain a persistent shopping cart per customer across sessions.
components.description: Stateless service that stores cart state in DynamoDB; supports add, update, remove, and retrieval operations.
inputs: Cart manipulation requests from API Gateway
security_considerations: Validate product IDs against Product Catalog Service

components.name: Order Service
components.purpose: Create, persist, and manage customer orders.
components.description: Stateless service that records orders, reserves inventory, and emits OrderCreated events for downstream processing.
security_considerations: Validate payment status before confirming order
scalability_considerations: Event‑driven order processing decouples load spikes

components.name: Payment Service
components.purpose: Process customer payments securely and report outcomes.
components.description: Stateless service that integrates with external payment providers, records transaction results, and publishes PaymentProcessed events.
security_considerations: TLS encryption for all external calls
scalability_considerations: Asynchronous event publishing avoids blocking checkout flow

components.name: Inventory Service
components.purpose: Track stock levels and enforce product availability constraints.
components.description: Stateless service that updates inventory counts, prevents overselling, and emits InventoryReserved events.
inputs: Inventory check requests from API Gateway
security_considerations: Validate order quantities against available stock
scalability_considerations: DynamoDB scales for high write throughput

components.name: Notification Service
components.purpose: Send email/SMS notifications for order confirmations, payment receipts, and shipment updates.
components.description: Consumes events from the Event Bus and triggers outbound messages via Amazon SES/SNS.
security_considerations: Ensure email content does not expose sensitive data
scalability_considerations: Lambda scales automatically with event volume

components.name: Event Bus
components.purpose: Provide asynchronous, decoupled communication between services.
components.description: Implemented with Amazon SNS topics and SQS queues; supports at‑least‑once delivery and fan‑out to multiple consumers.
outputs: Events delivered to Notification Service and other interested services
scalability_considerations: Managed service scales automatically with message volume

components.name: Data Store
components.purpose: Persist domain data for all services using DynamoDB.
components.description: A set of DynamoDB tables, each owned by a single service, providing low‑latency, highly available key‑value storage.
scalability_considerations: On‑demand capacity mode for unpredictable traffic
Global secondary indexes for query patterns

components.name: Cache
components.purpose: Accelerate read‑heavy product data and reduce DynamoDB load.
components.description: Redis cluster (ElastiCache) used for caching product listings and session data.
inputs: Cache get/set requests from API Gateway and services

components.name: Search Index
components.purpose: Store searchable product documents for full‑text queries.
components.description: OpenSearch domain containing indexed product data, refreshed from the Product Catalog Service.
inputs: Indexing updates from Product Catalog Service
outputs: Search result documents to Search Service
